item.title: Supermarket Cyber-Attack Highlights Vulnerabilities in Connected Devices
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?
Supermarkets across Europe faced a cyber-attack targeting fridges and freezers, raising concerns about vulnerabilities in internet-connected devices. While such systems can be remotely controlled, manufacturers typically implement security measures. Researchers previously demonstrated vulnerabilities in Samsung fridges, but no evidence links domestic appliances to the recent supermarket attacks. Ciaran Martin, former NCSC CEO, urged stronger security demands from tech companies and advised users to update devices and enable multi-factor authentication. UK law since April 2024 mandates cybersecurity standards for smart devices. The NCSC is investigating the supermarket incident but found no UK impact. UK Cyber Defence identified over 800 refrigeration systems accessible via the internet, potentially exposing them to attacks via weak passwords or software flaws. Helen Dickinson of the British Retail Consortium highlighted cyber risks for retailers. A 2025 ransomware attack on M&S and Co-op caused stock shortages. Tom Hegel emphasized the need for clear responsibility in securing connected equipment. Cybersecurity experts noted that while industries like automotive and utilities have improved security, smaller providers may still use outdated systems, leaving critical infrastructure vulnerable to similar risks.

item.title: European Supermarkets Hit by Cyberattack on Refrigeration Systems
item.description:
Source: BBC News, Deutsche Welle Original headline: European Supermarkets Face Second Cyberattack Targeting Refrigeration Systems
Supermarkets in seven European countries faced refrigeration system disruptions from a cyberattack using a method similar to a previous incident in France. The attack caused freezers and refrigerators to warm to 50C (122F), affecting dozens of stores in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia, and Finland. Sabcobel, a Belgian manufacturer, confirmed the attack involved switching evaporators to defrost mode, a technique linked to last month's French incident. CEO Stephan Moelans stated physical modifications were needed to secure systems, as many stores rely on internet-connected maintenance. In Sweden, ICA and Coop reported disruptions, with ICA noting temperatures spiked to 50C. Belgium’s prosecutor’s office opened a criminal investigation. Carref and Colruyt confirmed affected stores, while Ikea’s Mons location faced issues. The European Commission’s agriculture chief warned of deliberate attempts to disrupt food supplies. Sweden’s cybersecurity agency highlighted vulnerabilities in operational technology. The US is investigating similar malfunctions at military bases, though no UK incidents were reported. A Delhaize store in Flanders estimated €100,000 in losses from spoiled produce.

item.title: Poway, Rancho Bernardo newspapers win 13 San Diego Press Club awards
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune
The Poway News Chieftain and Rancho Bernardo News Journal won 13 awards at the San Diego Press Club’s 53rd annual Excellence in Journalism Awards ceremony on Oct. 27. All awards were in the non-daily newspapers division. Editor Elizabeth Marie Himchak earned eight honors, including first-place wins in feature-light subject, health and medicine, and sports categories. Judges praised her work, calling one a 'sweet story that shows the hustle behind two new influencers' and another 'an interesting look at one woman’s book about her son’s addiction to fentanyl and death.' Her sports piece on a Poway teacher running marathons was noted for 'relevant quotes from the marathoner and her husband.' Himchak also received second-place honors in environment and history, third-place in entertainment reporting and political/government, and an honorable mention in general news. Freelance photographer Criselda Yee won two awards, including 'Best of Show' for her photography. Reporter Julie Gallant and former editor Susan Gill Vardon received third-place series recognition. Freelance writer Amy Stark Shireman earned second-place honors in feature-light subject.

item.title: City Heights nonprofit opens San Diego County's first AI lab
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: City Heights nonprofit opens San Diego County's first AI lab to teach residents new technology skills
The City Heights Community Development Corporation opened San Diego County's first AI lab to teach residents new technology skills. The lab provides access to AI software like Co-Pilot and Claude, offering training on tasks such as budgeting and building small business loan models. Attendees like Austin Roth emphasized the importance of hands-on experience as AI evolves. Joseph Johnson noted the training fills a gap for aspiring entrepreneurs. Angel Stancer, vice president of workforce development, highlighted that such resources have typically been inaccessible to local residents. The lab, set to launch publicly by year's end, will host 90-minute workshops and a robotics room for engaging with emerging technologies. Stancer said the initiative aims to help residents stay competitive in the job market and break technology barriers.

item.title: North Korea Denies Involvement in Binance Hack, Calls U.S. Claims Provocative
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune, BBC News, Deutsche Welle Original headline: North Korea Denies Role in Binance Hack, Calls U.S. Accusations 'Provocation'
North Korea denies involvement in the $6.3 billion Binance hack, calling U.S. accusations a 'grave political provocation.' Kim Yo Jong, North Korea's leader's sister, criticized the FBI's claim that state-backed hackers orchestrated the attack, labeling it 'absurd rhetoric' and a 'sinister attempt' to harm Pyongyang's reputation. The FBI and cyber analysts attribute the breach to TraderTraitor, a group linked to a $1.5 billion Bybit hack in 2025. Binance confirmed $4.72 billion was stolen but has recovered 95% of the funds. North Korea faces longstanding accusations of using cybercrime to fund its economy and nuclear program, with South Korea's spy agency estimating $1.1 billion in stolen crypto over five years. Kim Yo Jong reiterated Pyongyang's stance against 'malicious acts in cyberspace' and warned of U.S. 'hostile attitude.' President Trump expressed uncertainty about North Korea's involvement. The incident follows recent North Korean weapons tests, including a new cluster warhead for cruise missiles, as the country seeks leverage in U.S. diplomacy. Seoul's Foreign Ministry highlighted the threat of North Korea's cyber operations to the global digital economy.
item.source: San Diego Union-Tribune, BBC News, Deutsche Welle

item.title: San Diego County lifts burn permit suspension
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Burn permit suspensions lifted in San Diego County
San Diego County Fire Chief Tony Mecham lifted the burn permit suspension Monday due to recent rains and cooler temperatures. Residents with valid agricultural or residential permits may resume burning on permissible days, which run 8 a.m. to sunset. Agricultural burns require Cal Fire inspections before ignition, while residential burns may also need inspections. Permits must be verified, and burn days must be confirmed before ignition. Safety guidelines mandate strict fire control, with civil or criminal liability for uncontrolled fires. Cal Fire emphasized that safe residential pile burning reduces fire hazards. State, federal, and local agencies will conduct prescribed burns on private and public lands during this period. Burning regulations details are available at burnpermit.fire.gov.

item.title: Local Officials Seek Federal Enforcement at La Jolla Cove
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Letter from local agencies seeks federal help, additional enforcement at La Jolla Cove
Local officials and a congressman have requested federal enforcement assistance to address harassment of sea lions at La Jolla Cove. A letter signed by San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria, City Council president Joe LaCava, California Coastal Commission executive director Kate Huckelbridge, and Congressman Scott Peters was submitted to NOAA Fisheries on Oct. 22. The letter asks for federal enforcement presence and delegated authority for the city to enforce the Marine Mammal Protection Act, which prohibits harassing sea lions. NOAA Fisheries director John Chu confirmed awareness of the letter. City rangers lack enforcement power under the MMPA, which only NOAA agents can enforce. The request follows a viral video showing a man kicking a sea lion in July, leading to a guilty plea from Tyler Muehl, 18. LaCava noted NOAA’s limited staffing and proposed deputizing city rangers to issue citations. The letter highlights ongoing challenges with repeat offenders despite educational efforts. Congressman Peters emphasized balancing public access with wildlife protection. NOAA’s response remains pending.

item.title: DoorDash Bans LinkedIn Connections with Instacart Employees Amid $17B Merger
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: DoorDash tells employees not to connect with Instacart peers on LinkedIn. It’s an uncommon M&A ask
DoorDash employees are prohibited from connecting with Instacart employees on LinkedIn as part of the company's $17 billion acquisition of Instacart. An internal SEC-filed Q&A document instructs employees not to request new connections or accept requests from Instacart staff, emphasizing the need to maintain separate operations until the deal closes, expected in late 2027 or early 2028. The restriction aims to prevent 'gun-jumping,' where employees act as if the merger is already complete, potentially leaking sensitive information or coordinating competitively. Legal experts note this is an unusual step, as M&A restrictions typically focus on internal practices rather than social media connections. Chris Selland, a business lecturer, warned that such limits could hinder talent mobility, while antitrust lawyer David Gelfand stressed the importance of maintaining independent competitor behavior. Some M&A experts called the LinkedIn ban unprecedented, though DoorDash did not comment on the matter. The move raises questions about its necessity versus overreach in antitrust compliance.

item.title: America's polarization is less extreme than perceived, with a large middle ground
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: Is America really that polarized? The answer might be a surprise
Shanna Berry and Alma Ong, friends with differing political views, unexpectedly agreed on Venezuela's situation. Berry, a Trump supporter, said the end of Maduro's regime was necessary, while Ong, a liberal, praised Berry's stance. Political researchers note America's polarization is less extreme than perceived. Kristin Laurin, a psychology professor, explained that people avoid political discussions, leading to overestimation of differences. Pew Research data shows 60% of Americans fall into a 'messy middle' with overlapping values, contrasting with 21% in extreme right groups. Former FBI director James Comey's indictment for a beach photo sparked bipartisan support for free speech. Researchers argue political divisions exist but many share common ground. Jocelyn Kiley of Pew noted the 'messy middle' is larger than ideological extremes, with nuanced views beneath party labels.

item.title: Russia Deploys Anti-Starlink Jammers in Parking Lots and Trailers
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Russia is hiding anti-Starlink jammers in parking lots and trailers on the front lines: Ukraine drone expert
Russia is deploying trailer-mounted anti-Starlink jammers to disrupt Ukraine's use of Starshield, according to Ukrainian drone expert Serhii Beskrestnov. Each jammer covers 25 square kilometers and targets satellites with dish antennas, creating interference that hinders Starlink connectivity. Russia has saturated key sites in Crimea and is expanding deployment along the front line to counter Ukraine's deep-recon missions. Beskrestnov warned Ukrainian drone pilots to watch for truck or trailer parking lots, noting that 3-6 of dozens of vehicles may hide the systems. The Volna Kupol Garant system, which uses generators to operate, now employs single-antenna trailers to conceal jammers. Ukraine first reported the system's use in Kharkiv in 2024, with increased deployment this year as Starshield enables deeper strikes. Analysts estimate Starshield uses at least 240 satellites, limiting each jammer to targeting one low-Earth-orbit satellite at a time. Russia's serial production of the system, reported by TASS in August, aims to bolster countermeasures against Ukraine's drone operations.

item.title: Amazon’s Tracy Warehouse Combines Robots and Workers
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: See inside Amazon’s robot warehouse
Amazon’s Tracy warehouse blends robotics and human labor. The 1.4 million square foot facility employs over 3,000 workers, up from 1,000 in 2023. Robots like Hercules carry inventory pods to workstations, while Robin and Cardinal handle package picking and loading. Pegasus and Proteus transport sorted items to outbound trucks. Human workers manage jams, damaged goods, and manual loading tasks. Process assistants like Briana Brager monitor systems and repair broken robots. A 'Jackpot' area redirects lost packages to human workers. Amazon claims next-gen centers are 25% more productive and support 30% more skilled jobs. Despite automation, manual tasks remain critical, with employees overseeing robotic systems and adjusting workflows as needed.

item.title: Solana Beach Starts Lomas Santa Fe Corridor East Improvements
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Solana Beach breaks ground on Lomas Santa Fe improvements
Solana Beach officials broke ground on the Lomas Santa Fe Corridor East Improvements Project on Oct. 28. Construction will span from Santa Helena Drive to Highland Drive, completing by fall 2027. The project includes paving, raised medians with drought-tolerant landscaping, two-way Class 2 bicycle lanes, a multiuse path on the north side, a sidewalk on the south side, trash/recycling containers, storm drain upgrades, and other features. City Engineer Austin Frisby outlined phased work starting with medians, followed by south-side sidewalks. North-side roadway improvements will add nearly 1 mile of scenic multiuse trail. Temporary lane closures, traffic control, and delays are expected during construction. Funding comes from a $7 million federal grant backed by Rep. Mike Levin and revenue from Measure S one-cent sales tax, totaling approximately $7.4 million. Updates will be posted on the city website.

item.title: Taiwan’s AI stock gains shift investor focus from startups to public markets
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Taiwan’s AI stock boom is making early-stage startups a harder sell
Taiwan’s AI stock boom has boosted public-market returns, making early-stage startups harder to fund. The Taiex index rose over 50% this year, outperforming South Korea’s Kospi. Investors are shifting toward listed AI stocks, with 35% of fund managers expecting Taiwan to benefit most from the next AI cycle. Anderson Chen, founder of Operon Solutions, raised $700,000 pre-seed funding from Silicon Valley investors, citing 10X stock market returns versus 2-3X from IPOs. Caleb Chu, an investor, noted Taiwanese investors favor B- and C-round deals with clearer returns. Findit data shows seed/angel rounds by Taiwanese VC firms dropped from 38.4% in 2021 to 17.1% in 2024. KPMG reported a 'crowding-out effect' for private funds due to TSMC’s stock strength. US data shows early-stage AI deals outperformed non-AI peers, contrasting with Taiwan’s trend. Founders like Chen are seeking overseas capital, with Operon’s round closing in three days. Chu said global investors favor early-stage bets, while Taiwan’s market favors public stocks.

item.title: Uganda withdraws troops from Somalia after 20 years
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Uganda begins withdrawing troops from Somalia after two decades
Uganda began withdrawing troops from Somalia after two decades of involvement. The Ugandan military confirmed the first cohort of troops had returned, marking the end of its 20-year peace and stabilization operations. Around 4,500 Ugandan soldiers are part of the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), with full withdrawal planned by 2027. The decision follows the U.S. ending funding for a UN logistics office critical to the mission, citing stalled progress against Al-Shabab. The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia also closed after 30 years, transferring responsibility to Somali authorities. Somalia faces challenges ahead of May 2024 elections, with Al-Shabab regaining territory and security concerns persisting. Uganda’s withdrawal allows Somali forces to assume full security responsibility, though militants continue to control central and southern regions.

item.title: Apple Can't Predict iPhone Duo Supply Catch-Up Timeline
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Apple says it's 'really hard' to predict when iPhone Duo supply will catch up to demand
Apple's chief operating officer Sabih Khan told investors during an earnings call that supply of the new iPhone Duo remains constrained, with no clear timeline for when demand will be met. The foldable phone, released on October 23 after preorders began on October 16, faces delivery delays extending into late January 2027. Khan emphasized that while the product's ramp is progressing, predicting supply-demand balance is 'really hard.' The supply issues extend to Macs and iPads, with memory constraints cited as the primary bottleneck for the December quarter. Apple competes with tech giants like Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron for memory chips, which are shifting toward AI data centers. Higher memory costs have reduced gross margins by about one percentage point. Despite these challenges, Apple reported $114.5 billion in revenue, with iPhone sales reaching $57.58 billion, exceeding Wall Street estimates.

item.title: European Nations Rehearse Ukraine Deployment in Peace Scenario
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Thousands of European troops to rehearse Ukraine deployment in event of peace
Britain and France will lead a military exercise in Poland involving nearly 3,000 troops from 12 European nations to test a multinational force's ability to deploy to Ukraine in the event of a peace deal. The exercise, named Exercise Koalicja, runs from November 9-22 and simulates logistics, command, and coordination for a potential force. Western officials emphasize the force would not engage in offensive operations, peacekeeping, or frontline combat, instead providing reassurance to Ukraine and aiding its military rebuilding. The US is not participating, while Russia opposes foreign troops in Ukraine, calling them 'legitimate targets.' Details on rules of engagement and force structure remain unclear. Participating nations include France, Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, Sweden, Turkey, and the UK, which contributes 300 troops and RAF Typhoons. Turkey leads the maritime mission to clear Black Sea mines. Officials acknowledge troop numbers and contributions depend on post-conflict conditions and political decisions. Ukraine's soldiers are already training NATO forces in drone warfare, though the training role for Ukrainian troops remains unspecified.

item.title: Apple CEO Ternus beats earnings but misses China and iPad sales
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: New CEO John Ternus delivers an Apple earnings beat — but China and iPad sales miss
Apple CEO John Ternus reported third-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion, exceeding Wall Street's $113.46 billion estimate, with earnings per share at $2.10, above forecasts. iPhone revenue hit $57.58 billion, while gross margin reached 47.9%, aided by tariff refunds. China revenue of $17.54 billion missed estimates of $18.75 billion, and iPad sales fell short at $6.23 billion versus $6.83 billion. Mac sales exceeded estimates at $10.79 billion, and Services revenue aligned with forecasts at $31.57 billion. Ternus acknowledged supply constraints and highlighted iPhone and Mac performance. Analysts noted broader concerns about non-iphone segments underperforming. The stock remained flat post-report. Apple's holiday quarter guidance showed slightly higher operating expenses than expected. Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook on September 1, announced new products like the iPhone Duo and MacBook Pro, though non-Pro iPhone variants are delayed. Rising memory costs and supply chain issues continue to pressure pricing strategies.

item.title: New AI rankings show China's open models lag behind U.S. rivals
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: A new way of measuring AI models suggests China's threat to OpenAI and Anthropic may have been overblown
Artificial Analysis revised its AI performance tests to reflect real-world usage, revealing a wider gap between open-weight Chinese models and U.S. closed models. Under the new system, the best open models trailed the top closed model by 12 points, compared to 3 points previously. Kimi K3.1 Pro and other open models scored 32 points, while Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 scored 58. Sridhar Ramaswamy noted the shift from 3 to 12-point gap, questioning if open models were catching up or if tests were flawed. Nathan Lambert admitted previous rankings may have overestimated open models. Dax Raad's analysis showed OpenRouter traffic could be handled by cheaper hardware, suggesting open models may not drive as much demand as feared. While open models remain competitive in areas like software development, the findings challenge claims of a looming Chinese AI threat to U.S. firms like OpenAI and Anthropic. The results could influence investment decisions for these companies' potential IPOs.

item.title: Poway Unified prioritizes reading instruction to boost student success
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Our Schools, Our Community: Student success starts with reading, and all of us have a role
Reading proficiency is critical for student success, with third graders not meeting reading standards four times more likely to miss high school graduation. Poway Unified School District emphasizes structured literacy, training over 450 general education teachers and 130 special education specialists since 2018. The district uses DIBELS screenings to identify reading challenges and organizes targeted instruction. In 2024-25, 72% of third graders met English language arts standards, compared to 44% statewide. Families are urged to engage in reading routines, discuss books, and support learning at home. Libraries and educators collaborate to ensure students develop reading skills across all grade levels. Superintendent Churchill highlights the need for early intervention and sustained support to prepare students for future challenges. The district’s approach combines explicit instruction, early identification, and community involvement to foster confident readers.

item.title: Mortgage Rates Drop to 7.07% APR on Monday, November 2
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Original headline: Mortgage Rates Today, Monday, November 2: Noticeably Lower
Mortgage rates fell to 7.07% APR on Monday, November 2, down 11 basis points from the prior day and 13 basis points from a week ago. The 30-year fixed-rate average, provided by Zillow to NerdWallet, remains above the 7% threshold. Analysts note that upcoming October jobs data and the Fed's December meeting could influence rates further. The September PCE inflation report showed 3.6% year-over-year inflation, up from 3.4% in August. A steady jobs report might support another Fed rate hike, affecting mortgage pricing. Refinancing advice suggests considering it if current rates are 0.5-0.75% lower than existing rates, with tools like NerdWallet's calculator to estimate savings. Rate locks are recommended if a favorable quote is secured, especially with float-down options. Discrepancies between online rates and personalized quotes stem from varying borrower profiles and market conditions. Lenders adjust rates frequently, so locking in a rate provides stability amid market fluctuations.

item.title: Karl Bushby returns to Hull after 28-year global trek
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Global pedestrian Karl Bushby returns home to UK after 28-year trek
British adventurer Karl Bushby returned to his hometown of Hull, England, after completing a 50,000-kilometer trek that began in Chile in 1998. The journey, which spanned 28 years, involved avoiding motorized transport and completing his goal before returning. Bushby faced numerous obstacles, including a 2006 near-fatal crossing of the iced Bering Strait with French explorer Dimitri Kieffer, visa refusals from Russia that extended his planned 12-year trip to over 25 years, and a 2020 pandemic delay. He also spent time in Panama jail for visa violations and lived in Mexico during lockdowns. Bushby reunited with his mother, son, and granddaughter in Hull. German filmmaker Werner Herzog is documenting the journey in a film titled 'Walk of Life.' Bushby expressed uncertainty about re-adjusting to normal life in an interview with AFP in September, stating, 'I've got to try and get established in the grown-up world again.'

item.title: Washington Resident Dies from Bird Flu After Cattle Exposure
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Washington state resident dies from bird flu following exposure to infected cattle
A Washington state resident died from complications of bird flu, marking the first U.S. death linked to the virus in a year. The individual, who had preexisting health conditions, was exposed to avian influenza at a dairy with infected cattle and died Sunday, according to Yakima County health officials. The CDC confirmed the strain was H5N1, the same variant responsible for an earlier U.S. death in Louisiana in January 2025. County officials reported 33 dairy herds testing positive for H5N1 and linked three human infections to dairy exposure. The CDC analyzed the virus from the Washington case and found no mutations increasing transmissibility or severity. Over 70 human infections have been reported in the U.S. since 2024, though no person-to-person spread has been documented. Officials warn farm workers and others handling poultry to take precautions, including protective gear, to reduce exposure risks.

item.title: SoCal shifts from Halloween storms to 80s temperatures
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: SoCal moves from Halloween storms to temperatures in the 80s
Southern California transitioned from Halloween storms to warmer temperatures in the 80s. Heavy rain over the weekend triggered flood advisories in Ventura, Orange, and San Diego counties, but no major flooding or mudslides occurred. Coastal areas faced beach hazard warnings due to gusty west winds and swells, with calmer conditions expected Tuesday and Wednesday. Active storm patterns in the north Pacific will bring northwest swells starting Thursday, peaking Saturday. Meteorologist Devin Black noted generally dry conditions and seasonal temperatures through Thursday, with weak Santa Ana winds increasing heat risk near the coast. Paul Steward predicted temperatures could reach mid-80s by week’s end, with potential wet weather returning mid-November. Rainfall varied, with Alhambra and Ventura-Oxnard areas receiving up to 1.5 inches. Flood advisories were lifted after the weekend’s rain, though some minor coastal impacts were reported.

item.title: El Niño Intensifies Storms and Floods in Southwest
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Is El Niño making storms and flash floods in the Southwest worse?
El Niño is intensifying storms and flash floods in the Southwest, according to experts. The extreme climate phenomenon is fueling heavier rains by adding moisture to the atmosphere and altering wind patterns. Meteorologist Jeff Masters called it a 'super duper El Niño,' noting its impacts will persist for months. Flash floods prompted evacuations in northern New Mexico, central Arizona, and Colorado, while over 20 trillion gallons of water fell on the Four Corners states and Nevada in two weeks. Climate scientist Daniel Swain said the Southwest is experiencing unprecedented precipitation levels. Warmer ocean temperatures due to human-caused climate change are amplifying El Niño effects, making extreme weather more likely. The event is expected to peak in December, intensifying storms across the western U.S. Experts warn of continued heavy rainfall and flooding, urging preparedness. While El Niño can replenish water resources, it also poses risks to communities. Meteorologist Randy Cerveny emphasized that the Pacific Ocean’s warming trend means 'more of these particular events' are likely.

item.title: San Diego County Proposes Sand and Rock to Protect Rail Corridor
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: More beach sand, rock placements proposed to protect San Diego County’s vulnerable railroad corridor
Transit agencies Metrolink and Orange County Transit Authority seek approval to reinforce rock revetments and add sand to protect a critical rail corridor linking San Diego to Los Angeles. The California Coastal Commission’s staff recommends approving the coastal development permit ahead of its Thursday board meeting. Environmental groups like Save Our Beaches oppose rock riprap, arguing it occupies public space and accelerates erosion. The staff report highlights the rail’s strategic importance for freight and travel, noting increased vulnerability to sea level rise and El Niño storms since 2021. Rail closures due to erosion have become frequent, prompting 15 stabilization projects since 2021. While sand replenishment is favored for its temporary protection and recreational benefits, rock revetments face criticism for long-term erosion risks. Save Our Beaches urges the commission to limit rock use and prioritize sand replenishment. The proposed work targets two sites near San Clemente Pier, with a history of sand placement dating to 1928.

item.title: CCA Hack Club hosts free gaming event Nov. 14-15
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune
CCA Hack Club is hosting a free game development event for teens aged 13-18 at Canyon Crest Academy on Nov 14-15. The game jam, organized by the club, is open to all North County high school students and aims to promote accessibility to technology and creative computing while fostering community connections. The club previously hosted a smaller game jam in February 2023 through Games for Change, but Haven North County seeks to attract over 40 participants. The event includes programming and design workshops, with registration available at haven.hackclub.com/nc-san-diego. The club, established two years ago, emphasizes collaboration and skill-building among students interested in game development.

item.title: Federal judge orders Iowa to allow Satanic Temple holiday event in Capitol
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Federal judge orders Iowa to allow Satanic Temple to hold one-day holiday event in the state Capitol
A federal judge ordered Iowa state officials to permit the Satanic Temple to hold a holiday event in the state Capitol rotunda after rejecting their application for years. The ruling follows a lawsuit by the group and its Iowa chapter, which argued state officials discriminated against their religion by denying the event. Judge Stephanie M. Rose ruled the state’s claims about child safety and potential weaponization of sticks were not valid grounds to block the event. The Satanic Temple’s display would include Krampus costumes, caroling, and family activities. State officials had previously cited policies against gratuitous violence and obscene displays, but the judge said those concerns could not justify denying free speech. The group’s application was rejected in 2024. The American Civil Liberties Union of Iowa represents the group in the case. The Satanic Temple’s attorney, Matt Kezhaya, called the event family-friendly and criticized state officials for mischaracterizing their expression. Iowa’s Department of Administrative Services and Gov. Kim Reynolds did not immediately comment.

item.title: Donna Gustafson Survives Pancreatic Cancer with mRNA Vaccine
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: This woman defied lethal cancer. Can mRNA vaccines make that possible for others?
Donna Gustafson, 72, survived Stage II pancreatic cancer after receiving an mRNA vaccine seven years ago. She was part of a trial with 16 patients, where the vaccine worked on half, including her. The treatment, combining mRNA, genomics, and AI, reprograms immune cells to target cancer proteins. Merck and Moderna reported a 42% reduction in skin cancer recurrence with mRNA vaccines. Researchers like Vinod Balachandran note the vaccine's durability, with Gustafson's immune cells showing a 10,000-fold increase in cancer-attacking cells. The National Cancer Institute is partnering with private firms to accelerate mRNA vaccine development. Gustafson, who received nine doses alongside surgery and chemo, credits her daughters for enrolling her. She now leads an active life, including skydiving and traveling, with her husband Ed. The success highlights mRNA's potential for broader cancer treatments, though challenges remain in understanding trial variability.

item.title: Private jet likely broke apart before Florida crash killing all nine on board
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Jet may have broken apart before Florida crash, officials say, as family named among victims
Investigators believe parts of a private jet that crashed in Florida may have broken apart in the air before impact. The Learjet 60, en route from Austin, Texas to the Bahamas, nosedived into a highway in Palm Beach, killing all nine on board. The NTSB cited weather conditions as a key focus, noting heavy rainfall and thunderstorms at the time. Recovery efforts are hindered by a crater formed by the crash, partially filled with water. Cockpit audio reveals the crew reported turbulence, ice management, and a rapid descent of 10,000 feet per minute before declaring an emergency. Victims include tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, their children, and others. The pilot, Jeff Gregory, and copilot Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, died. Family statements describe Robinson and Sharp as devoted parents, while Filgueiras’ mother confirmed her death. The NTSB noted debris scattered across nearby areas and the possibility of aircraft parts found away from the impact site. Officials are seeking to locate a cockpit voice recorder.

item.title: San Diego seeks to allow childcare centers near job hubs
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: San Diego battling to allow childcare centers near key job centers in University City, Sorrento Valley
San Diego City Council voted 6-0 to override a county ban on new childcare centers in areas near key job centers like University City and Sorrento Valley. The move aims to address a childcare crisis, with the city classified as a childcare desert. The county’s Airport Land Use Commission previously rejected the zoning change, citing safety concerns during aviation emergencies. Councilmembers argued that childcare costs are a major burden for families and that proximity to jobs is critical. Councilmember Kent Lee emphasized that the transition zone, where the change applies, includes existing commercial areas and that noise rules still apply. Sean Elo-Rivera highlighted the need for accessible childcare, noting job growth in the area. The proposal now moves to the Planning Commission for review, with final approval expected in January. Officials from MCAS Miramar and the state Department of Transportation will provide input. The city has previously overridden similar restrictions for other developments near the airport.
